opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important question, because so far a lot of the conversation around homogeneity has been fairly narrow. People worry about model collapse: if you keep training models on synthetic data generated by other models, the distribution narrows, the tails disappear, and performance eventually degrades. That's real and worth studying, but I think it's only one slice of the problem.

The bigger issue, to me, is what happens to *people* and to *society* when so much of what we read, write, and think starts flowing through a small number of models that tend to produce similar outputs. If you ask a dozen different LLMs an open-ended question, like "write me a poem about the ocean" or "what should I consider in this ethical dilemma," you often get answers that are strikingly alike. They're fluent and reasonable, but they converge on the same safe, average, consensus-flavored response. Now imagine that happening across millions of students writing essays, professionals drafting documents, and people seeking advice. Over time, you could see a flattening of human expression and maybe even human thought.

So I think research needs to extend in a few directions.

First, measuring homogeneity in human outcomes, not just model outputs. Does the writing of people who use these tools heavily become more similar to each other? Do their opinions converge? Do they lose some of their distinctive voice? There's early evidence suggesting yes, at least for writing, but we need much more careful, longitudinal study.

Second, pluralism. Human values and perspectives are genuinely diverse. Cultures differ, communities differ, individuals differ, and many questions have no single right answer. When we align models toward one notion of "helpful" or "good," we often implicitly collapse that diversity into something resembling the average preference of a particular group of annotators. I'd like to see research on models that can represent and respect a spectrum of reasonable viewpoints rather than defaulting to one.

Third, creativity and the long tail. A lot of what makes human culture rich lives in the long tail: unusual ideas, minority perspectives, weird art. Our training objectives and decoding strategies tend to favor high-probability outputs, which pushes against that tail. So there's a technical question of how we build systems that can be genuinely diverse and surprising without becoming incoherent.

And finally, the epistemic ecosystem as a whole. If everyone consults the same oracle, we lose the healthy disagreement and independent reasoning that science and democracy depend on. That's not just a machine learning problem. It needs people from the social sciences, the humanities, and policy at the table.

So yes, model collapse matters, but I'd frame the larger research agenda as protecting diversity, of models, of ideas, and of people, as AI becomes more central to how we think.

r001.rationale: The response says that a dozen different LLMs often give strikingly alike answers to open-ended questions.

r002.rationale: It asks whether heavy use of these tools makes people’s writing more similar and their opinions converge, and describes a possible flattening of human thought.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the conversation about homogeneous output has been pretty narrowly framed so far. Most of the work I see is about model collapse, right? You train on synthetic data, the distribution narrows, you lose the tails, and eventually the model degrades. And that's a real concern, I don't want to dismiss it. But to me that's actually the least interesting part of the story, because it's a problem that's mostly internal to the people building these systems, and they have a lot of incentive to solve it.

What I think we're under-studying is the effect on humans. If hundreds of millions of people are writing with the same assistant, brainstorming with the same assistant, getting their first draft from the same assistant, then the homogeneity isn't just in the model's output anymore. It's in the emails people send, the essays students turn in, the code that gets committed. And it's subtle, because every individual output looks fine. It's perfectly fluent, it's reasonable. It's only when you zoom out that you notice everybody is converging on the same phrasings, the same argument structures, the same "safe" ideas.

And there's some early evidence on this that I find pretty striking. When people use these tools for creative tasks, individual quality often goes up, but the collective diversity of what the group produces goes down. So you get this weird trade where everyone is a little better and everyone is a lot more alike. I think that should worry us more than it does, because a lot of what makes culture and science work is the variance. The weird idea in the tail that turns out to matter.

So concretely, I'd want research in a few directions. One is measurement. We have very good metrics for whether an output is correct or helpful, and really bad metrics for whether a population of outputs is diverse in a meaningful sense, not just lexically. Two is the feedback loop between people and models, because people adapt to the model and then the model is trained on people who've adapted to it, and we don't understand that dynamic at all. And three, honestly, is the alignment side. A lot of the homogeneity is a direct consequence of how we do RLHF. We optimize for the mode of what annotators like, and the mode is, by construction, the least surprising thing. So I'd like to see alignment research that treats pluralism as a first-class objective, not as something you hope survives the training process.

r001.rationale: The response describes outputs and people converging around the same assistant, but does not say that different LLMs give similar answers to the same open-ended question.

r002.rationale: It discusses people adapting to assistants and producing more similar work, but does not ask whether exposure to homogeneous LLM content makes human thinking more homogeneous.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to look at what happens to human thinking, too. If millions of people are using these systems to brainstorm, to write, to explore a question, and the systems keep suggesting similar ideas, does that make our own thinking more homogeneous over time? You can have an individual who feels more creative or productive with AI, while the diversity of ideas across people actually decreases.

So I would want to study that interaction over time. Which perspectives do people encounter? Which possibilities do they stop considering? And do they become more willing to question an answer, or more likely to accept it because it sounds fluent and reasonable?

The goal shouldn't just be to make the model produce more varied wording. It's to understand whether these systems help people develop different ideas and exercise their own judgment. That's a much broader question than what happens when we train the next model on their output.

r001.rationale: The response says systems may keep suggesting similar ideas, but does not state that different LLMs often give similar answers to the same open-ended question.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks whether repeated exposure to similar AI suggestions makes people’s own thinking more homogeneous over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to look at what happens to people when they interact with these systems, not just what happens when we train the next model on their outputs. If we all use language models that suggest similar ideas, similar ways of writing, similar ways of framing a problem, does that make our own thinking more homogeneous over time?

That’s especially interesting for creativity. An AI assistant might help an individual produce something better, but if everybody gets steered toward the same kinds of answers, we could lose diversity collectively. Those two effects can coexist.

So I’d love to see more longitudinal studies of how people’s ideas and judgments change with repeated use, and whether different designs help preserve independent thinking. We should ask not only whether the system gives a useful answer, but whether it helps people explore possibilities they otherwise wouldn’t have considered.
